idiom_name: generic class-expression mixins (methods only); operators cannot be overloaded and types are erased
implementation_notes: TypeScript cannot overload operators - the type system has no hooks for +, < or ==, and the JavaScript coercion hooks (Symbol.toPrimitive, valueOf) return primitives - so an operator family can never be supplied to a family of types. What does exist is the class-expression mixin pattern: a generic function typed as function Base<TBase extends Constructor>(Base: TBase) { return class extends Base { ... } } composes behaviour into a family of classes while the compiler infers the intersection instance type (Constructor<T> = new (...args: any[]) => T, with GConstructor<T> to constrain the base). Use that for behaviour mixins and expose comparison as ordinary API - compareTo, equals, or a Comparable<T> interface consumed by generic helpers - so that the absence of operator syntax is explicit rather than accidental.
alternative: Generic class-expression mixins for shared behaviour plus explicitly named comparison API (compareTo, equals, valueOf-based key extraction) and helper functions over a Comparable<T> interface; TypeScript has no operator hooks, and a + b on class instances silently coerces instead of compiling to your semantics.
pitfalls: Class-expression mixin types are inferred as intersections and get unwieldy fast; explicit Constructor<T>/GConstructor<T> annotations are needed, and declarations with private or protected members can break the mixin typing.
Because operators cannot be hooked, a + b on class instances silently coerces to a string or NaN instead of failing - the exact place where C++ code being ported expects a compile error.

Mixin copies performed by Object.assign at runtime are invisible to the type checker unless the intersection type is declared by hand, so the compiler can believe a method exists that was never copied.
